full_judgment:
“Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 

 With reference to the above quoted Memo, I beg to state for your information that the above named accused is detained in this jail as per Govt. Order No. 737-See. (1) dated 2-10-73 under section (1) of section 17 of the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 (Ordinance No LXXIII of 1958). 

 As, after perusing the above report, the learned Sessions Judge felt unable to do anything in view of the alleged order of detention under the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958, the petitioner moved this Court under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 4. An affidavit in opposition was filed by a Section Officer, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh which contested the statements made by the petitioner. It was stated that the petitioner was an active member of the so-called "Islami Samajbadi Muslim Bangla Biplobi Sarkar" formed in June, 1972, by A.K. Habibur Rahman alias General Habib Khan. The said General who is the Chief of the organization disclosed in his confession that the petitioner financed him in carrying out the Muslim Bangla Movement. The petitioner was initially arrested on 28-5-73 in connection with Sutrapur P.S. (Dacca) Case No. 23(5) 73 under section 19A (f) of the Arms Act read with P.O. No. 50/70. The petitioner was subsequently arrested on 3-9-73 under section 41(1) of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance, 1958. For these reasons when the learned Sessions Judge, Dacca ordered the petitioner's release on bail on 5-9-73 he could not be released. In the same affidavit-in-opposition it was asserted that on 3-9-73 the petitioner was shown arrested under section 41 of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance and with effect from 2-10-73 he was shown detained under section 17(1) of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance by the Government. The grounds of detention were communicated to the petitioner. A fresh order under section 17 (1) of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance was issued on 2-1-74 detaining the petitioner for three months with effect from this date. It was further stated that the order dated 2-1-74 relating to the detention of the petitioner was rescinded on 31-1-74. It was, therefore, submitted that the Rule has become infractions. In a supplementary affidavit on behalf of the State filed on 20-2-74 it was stated that after the order of detention dated 2-1-74 was rescinded by the President on 31-1-74 the petitioner was released from the custody and was arrested, again by virtue of a fresh order dated 1-2-74 and the petitioner was being detained under, this order for a period of three months; This order was annexed to the supplementary affidavit an annexure 'A' which runs as follows: 

 Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 

 NOW, THEREFORE, in exercise of the power conferred by clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 (Ordinance No. LXXVIII of 1958), the President is pleased to direct that the said person be detained for a period of 3 (three) months from the date of service of this order on him. 

 5. In his affidavit in reply the petitioner maintained that detention is illegal and mala fide and it was submitted by him that he was detained under section 41 of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 with effect from 6-9-73 after the bail bond was received. He submitted that since under an order of detention passed on 2-1-74 he was still being held in detention, the Rule has not become infractions, particularly when the fact is that he was never released from the custody as stated above by the Government in the supplementary affidavit. 

 6. Mr. Kazi Shahadat Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted, firstly that the initial order of detention of the petitioner being illegal the same cannot be validated by a subsequent order of detention under sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance, 1958. Secondly, since the satisfaction under section 17(1) of the Ordinance is to be that of the Government, the impugned order of detention which is alleged to have been passed on the satisfaction of the President of the Republic is illegal. Finally, the grounds supplied to the petitioner are vague which did not permit the petitioner to make an effective representation against the same and on the materials upon which such grounds were made out the detaining authority cannot be said to have been reasonably satisfied. In this connection, it was further submitted that no grounds were served along with the orders of detention passed on 1-1-74 and 1-2-74 respectively. The circumstances leading to the arrest of the petitioner and the manner in which the detaining authority proceeded show the mala fide nature of the action. Before proceeding further the relevant provisions of sections 17(1) and 41 of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance may be quoted. Provisions of section 17(1) are as follows : 

 “17 (1) The.............Government, if satisfied with respect to any particular person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, may make an order (a) directing that he be detained.” 

 7. Section 41 of the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 runs as follows: 

 “41.(1) Any police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector or any other officer of Government empowered in this behalf by general or special order of the..........Government, may arrest without warrant any person whom he reasonably suspects of having done, or of doing, or of being about to do, a prejudicial act.” 

 8. The scope of the power of the Police to arrest on reasonable suspicion on the Government to order detention or being satisfied that a person is indulging if any prejudicial activities as provided, under the aforesaid provision or provisions similar to those has been considered in a number of decisions, the latest being the case of (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 403-Golam Jilani Vs. The Government of West Pakistan, reported in P.L.D. 1967 (SC) 373 and the case of Abdul Baki Vs. The Government of Pakistan, reported in (1963) 20 DLR (SC) 249; P.L.D. 1968 (SC) 313 and the case of Government of West Pakistan and another Vs. Begum Agha Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri, (1969) 21 DLR (SC) reported in P.L.D. 1969. (SC) 14. All these cases dealt with the question regarding the reasonableness of satisfaction of the detaining authority and sufficiency of materials upon which the grounds for a person's detention were made out and the satisfaction of the detaining authority was derived. 

 10. As under President's Order No. 48 of 1972 certain adaptations to the existing laws were made, the expression "Provincial Government" in sections 17 and 41 of the Ordinance is to be construed as a reference to the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 Facts as they have emerged from the petition and the counter-affidavit and affidavit in reply, revealed a few things which, as has been claimed by the petitioner, tend to undermine the very basis of the action of the detaining authority and cannot succeed to establish that the petitioner is being validly detained. The petitioner had admittedly been in jail since 28-5-73 in connection with a case under Arms Act and he was ordered to be released on bail by the learned Sessions Judge, Dacca on 5-9-73, As appears from the reply dated 4-12-73 of the D.I.G., Prisons, Dacca which has been quoted above it is seen that the D.I.G. is referring to the order of detention dated 2-10-73 under section 17(1) of the Bangladesh Public Safety Ordinance. Almost a month had elapsed since the learned Sessions Judge ordered the release of the petitioner before this order seems to have been passed on 2-10-73. It is inexplicable why the D.I.G. Prisons, choose to be discreetly silent about the petitioner's position during the period beginning from 6-9-73 the date on which the order of releasing the petitioner on bail granted by the learned Sessions Judge was communicated to him till the order of detention passed on 2-10-73. It now transpires from the affidavit-in-opposition that an earlier order was passed on 3-9-73 by a Police Officer under section 41(1) of the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958. This order has not, however, been annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition but has been merely mentioned therein. If such an order actually existed on or before the date on which the petitioner was granted bail by the learned Sessions Judge, Dacca, the D.I.G. Prisons did not know about it and no mention was made of the existence of such order in his report to the learned Sessions Judge. It seems curious that though he did not know the existence of such an order he refused to release the petitioner even after the learned Sessions Judge ordered his release on bail. When the petitioner is already in jail in connection with the case under Arms Act started as earlier as May, 1973, how could an order of arrest be made by the Police Officer under section 41(1) of the Public Safety Ordinance. Finding this difficulty in justifying the odd claim to have arrested a person in jail under section 41(1) of the public Safety ordinance, 1958, which provides that any police officer may arrest without warrant any person whom he reasonably suspects of having done, or of doing, or of being about to do, a prejudicial act, it has been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner was shown as arrest ted under the aforesaid section. It is undoubtedly an affront to one's credibility that the police could "reasonably suspect that a person like the petitioner who was already in jail has done or is doing or about to do a prejudicial act as defined in the Ordinance. If the petitioner was actually released and some time elapsed before he was arrested by the police under the aforesaid section it might have been justified in claiming to exercise the valid powers of arrest but since this is not the case here it can in no way be conceded that the police could entertain any reasonable suspicion about the petitioner that he has done or in doing or about to do a prejudicial act Moreover, on an examination of the provisions of section 41(1) it appears that the section conferred the powers of arrest without a warrant upon the police officer if he reasonably suspects in the circumstances mentioned therein but they do not, it is quite apparent, enable him to show as arrested a person who had been arrested three months ago in connection with another case. Since, as already mentioned, the order passed under section 41(1) of the Ordinance has not been placed before us, we cannot make any further comment on it. The whole approach seems to be questionable particularly in view of the lack of sufficient materials upon which the police can be said to have entertained reasonable suspicion regarding the petitioner's conduct or activities. Excepting the confession of the self-styled "General" Habib Khan which finds mention in the forwarding note of the Inspector of Police to the S.D.O. (S), Dacca, which has been quoted in full above, no other facts have been placed before us to show that the petitioner was indulging or about to indulge in any prejudicial act as defined in the Ordinance. Since the confession is not before us it not known what kind of confession it was, how it was made or what are its contents. The petitioner is a Contractor by profession and it is stated that he has no taste for politics particularly politics of a kind which the philosophy of armed revolution involves and in the case of a person like him it would require stronger and more convincing allegation to establish that he is connected with the activities whose aim is to overthrow the government through violent means. 

 11. Above all, the petitioner appears to have been involved in a case under the Arms Act as soon as he filed a case of dacoity against some miscreants including a son of highly placed official in the district of Sylhet from where the petitioner comes. Since the petitioner was arrested in May, 1973, apart from the confession of so-called "General" Habib Khan no other information or materials involving the petitioner in the Muslim Bangla movement was before the police which could make him reasonably suspect the petitioner that he is indulging or likely to indulge in any prejudicial act as defined in the Ordinance. It cannot, therefore, be said that the police had any basis upon which he could entertain "reasonable suspicion" against the petitioner for any act unless there were materials, other than the confession, in the possession of the police to show that he could entertain such suspicion. How can he be allowed powers to arrest a person without a warrant on the mere confession of another person arrested on the charge of a very grave offence, such as the overthrowing the Government of this country by violent means. If this is permissible there would be an end to the liberty of a citizen of Bangladesh which has been declared as his inalienable right, under the Constitution of Bangladesh. Any citizen could then be arrested on the ground that he has been implicated by some prisoner while confessing his guilt. We, therefore find it extremely difficult to say that even if the order dated 3-9-73 existed it could have been validly made by the police in the circumstances mentioned above. 

 13. Our attention was drawn to a portion of the order of detention which speaks of the President's satisfaction, the expressions used being "whereas the President is satisfied". The relevant section, i.e., section 17(1) of the Public Safety Ordinance mentions about the satisfaction of the government and not the satisfaction of the President. As the expressions "Government, if satisfied'' which occur in section 17(1) of the Ordinance do not and cannot mean and refer to the satisfaction of the President the recital in the order of detention dated 1-2-74 "Whereas the President is satisfied" is without any basis. If the aforesaid expressions should mean the satisfaction of the President the government must expressly empower the President to exercise power as we understood has been done and which, in our opinion, can never be done. The satisfaction referred to in section 17(1) must be reasonable satisfaction of a known person, the expression "Government if satisfied" is not a mere incantation or a convenient formula to enable the utilization of the high office of the President for the purposes of the section. Since the President has, apart from the circumstances mentioned in Article 48(3) of the Constitution, to act on the advice of the Prime Minister, his satisfaction cannot be actually his. A feeble, attempt was sought to be made to justify the recital "Whereas the President is satisfied" by taking resort to the provision of Article 55(4) of the Constitution which provides: 

 “(4) All executive actions of the Government shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.” 

 This provision cannot, we are afraid, be used to cure the inherent lack of power of the President to derive satisfaction under section 17 (1) of the Ordinance. To carry on the administration of the country in the name of the President as mentioned in Article 55(4) of the Constitution is one thing, to say that the President is satisfied, for the purpose of exercising power under Section 17 (1) of the Ordinance is something quite different. We, therefore, find it difficult to understand whose satisfaction it was that was being conveyed by the recital "Whereas the President is satisfied" or whose satisfaction it really was that must be accepted as equivalent to the satisfaction of the government as mentioned in the section. Whoever he is, he must be expressly authorized by an appropriate order to derive such satisfaction, as is referred to in section 17, which will enable him to make an order under clause (1) of that section. It becomes, therefore, apparent that in the circumstances as above mentioned, the President's satisfaction could not be accepted as the satisfaction of the government. As a result, the whole basis of the order of detention purported to have been made on the satisfaction of the President is gone. If the basis is no longer there the order must be deemed to have no validity and it must accordingly fall. 

 (a) any order or any action taken or anything done or any action taken or any proceeding commenced under any provision of the Security Act 1952 (XXXV of 1952), or the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 (E.P. Ord. LXXVIII of 1958), shall, in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be deemed to have been made, done, taken or commended under the corresponding provisions of this Act.
